what_worked: Strong thesis-driven narrative arc from concentration to geography to pricing inefficiency, with a clear landing.
fix_next: Slide 4 category counts and medians are badly wrong (e.g., SaaS 437 vs. actual 66, AI 392 vs. 197); verify every number against the dataset.
verdict: Compelling thesis undermined by fabricated-looking category figures on the key slide.
factual_error_detail: Slide 4: SaaS count 437 (actual 66), AI count 392 (actual 197), Productivity 275 (actual 49), Marketing 159 (actual 42), Analytics 131 (actual 19), E-comm 56 (actual 19). Medians also wrong: SaaS $527 (actual $200.50), AI $490 (actual $503), Productivity $328 (actual ~$80), Marketing $1,277 (actual $2,369.50), Analytics $886 (actual $419), E-comm $306 (actual $387). Slide 3: US 63% revenue claim and 26% startup share are unverifiable but plausible given 241 missing country values—no acknowledgment of missingness. Slide 5: 2.3x median multiple is close to reference B2B/B2C medians (~2.3x) so acceptable; 0.09 correlation is unverifiable but plausible.

evidence.insight: The concentration thesis (slide 2) and pricing-inefficiency angle (slide 5) go beyond chart description and offer a decision-relevant frame for a buyer/investor audience. However, the category crowding insight on slide 4 is built on wrong numbers, undermining its value.
evidence.narrative: Clear three-act structure: concentration exists (slide 2), it pools geographically (slide 3), categories show crowding vs. returns (slide 4), exit pricing is inefficient (slide 5), synthesis (slide 6). The landing on slide 6 ties back to the thesis. Sequence is purposeful.
evidence.framing: Title slide sets up the question well. Audience (capital allocators) is implicit but clear by slide 6. However, no mention of dataset limitations: 241 missing countries, 274 missing categories, 286 missing domains. The 26% US startup share is computed on a denominator that excludes ~24% of rows with missing country—never disclosed.
evidence.accuracy: Slide 2 stats (49.6% top-10 share, 21.6% zero-revenue) are correct. Slide 4 is catastrophically wrong: every category count is inflated by roughly 3-7x (total shown ~1,450 vs. actual 726 categorized), and medians diverge substantially from reference values. This is the analytical centerpiece slide and it fails.
evidence.visual: Consistent red/grey palette, clean typography, good use of big-number callouts. Bar charts are legible and well-labeled. The stacked bar on slide 2 is effective. Slide 4 uses a smart paired-chart layout. No chart junk. Slightly repetitive three-card template across slides 2 and 5.
evidence.ai_slop: The inflated category counts on slide 4 look like AI hallucination—numbers don't match any reasonable filter of the dataset. The consulting-style 'The read:' box on slide 5 borders on filler but contains a substantive claim.
